title: Write a root cause analysis and remediation plan
description: Project: Write a root cause analysis and remediation plan. Build and understand this project with step-by-step guidance.

data.text: A root cause analysis is not a blame document; it is a learning document. It records what happened, why it happened, and what the team will change to prevent recurrence. This lesson covers the RCA process, the 5 Whys technique, remediation prioritization, and how to write an incident postmortem that stakeholders can act on.

items: Gather timeline data from metrics, logs, and traces before forming conclusions
Identify the trigger event and the contributing factors that allowed it to become an incident
Apply the 5 Whys or fishbone diagram to move from symptoms to systemic causes
Distinguish between proximate cause and root cause; the proximate cause is what broke, the root cause is why it was allowed to break
Prioritize remediation items by risk reduction and implementation effort
Assign owners and deadlines to every action item

terms.definition: The fundamental reason a failure occurred, which if addressed would have prevented the incident entirely.
A condition or decision that made the incident worse or harder to detect, but was not the sole trigger.
An incident review that focuses on systems and processes rather than individual fault, encouraging honest reporting.
A prioritized list of actions to fix the root cause, mitigate contributing factors, and improve detection.
A specific, assigned task with a deadline that advances the remediation plan.

data.text: The 5 Whys is deceptively simple but easy to misuse. Stopping at the first answer produces a proximate cause, not a root cause. Continue asking why until you reach a systemic issue that the team can fix. If the answer is 'human error,' ask why the system allowed that human to make the error.

data.title: 5 Whys applied to a broken deployment
data.content: Proximate cause: a bad configuration value was deployed. Root cause: the pipeline did not validate configuration schemas.
data.code:
Why 1: Why did the deployment break?
-> The app failed to start because a config value was missing.

Why 2: Why was the config value missing?
-> The CI pipeline did not validate config against the expected schema.

Why 3: Why did the pipeline not validate config?
-> There is no schema validation step in the deployment workflow.

Why 4: Why is there no validation step?
-> The team did not include config validation in the definition of done.

Why 5: Why was it not in the definition of done?
-> The team does not have a checklist for deployment readiness.

Root cause: Missing deployment readiness checklist and config validation in CI.

items: Write the executive summary first: what happened, impact, duration, and resolution
Provide a detailed timeline with timestamps, actions taken, and who was involved
Present the root cause analysis with evidence from metrics, logs, and traces
List remediation items with clear owners, deadlines, and success criteria
Publish within 48 hours while the details are fresh; delayed postmortems lose accuracy

cards.title: Narrative postmortem
cards.description: A chronological story of the incident with context and analysis.
pros: Easy to read for non-technical stakeholders
cons: Harder to scan for action items

cards.title: Template-based postmortem
cards.description: A structured document with predefined sections for timeline, impact, root cause, and action items.
cons: May encourage box-checking over deep analysis

cards.title: Blameless retrospective
cards.description: A facilitated discussion focused on system improvements rather than fault.
cons: May not produce a formal written record

data.caption: Root cause analysis and remediation plan flow
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Incident resolved] --> B[Gather evidence]
    B --> C[Build timeline]
    C --> D[Identify trigger]
    D --> E[Apply 5 Whys]
    E --> F{Root cause found?}
    F -->|No| G[Expand investigation]
    F -->|Yes| H[Identify contributing factors]
    H --> I[Prioritize remediation]
    I --> J[Assign owners and deadlines]
    J --> K[Write postmortem]
    K --> L[Review with team]
    L --> M[Publish and track action items]

    note right of E
        Continue until you reach
        a systemic fix, not a
        proximate cause.
    end note

    note right of I
        High risk + low effort = do first.
        High risk + high effort = plan carefully.
    end note

data.title: Postmortems without action items are wasted effort
data.text: An incident postmortem that documents the failure but assigns no owner to any fix will be repeated. Every remediation item needs a name, a deadline, and a follow-up review. Track them in the same backlog as features.

items: Send an initial status update within 30 minutes of incident declaration
Follow up every 30 to 60 minutes with a brief progress note during active incidents
Tailor technical depth to the audience: engineers need root cause; executives need impact and timeline
Acknowledge uncertainty; do not speculate about causes you have not verified
Close the communication loop with a final summary and next steps within 24 hours

items.question: How long should a postmortem be?
items.answer: Long enough to answer the key questions and short enough that people will read it. One to three pages is typical. If it exceeds five pages, consider whether the investigation found too many unrelated issues or if the timeline is too detailed.

items.question: What if the root cause is a third-party service?
items.answer: The root cause may be external, but the contributing factors are internal. Ask why your system did not degrade gracefully when the third-party failed. Remediation should focus on resilience, not just on blaming the vendor.

items.question: How do I make the postmortem blameless?
items.answer: Focus on systems and processes. Replace 'the engineer forgot to run the test' with 'the test was not required by the deployment checklist.' The goal is to fix the environment that allowed the mistake, not the person who made it.

data.title: Write a postmortem for a recent incident
data.description: Pick a real or simulated incident from your experience. Write a postmortem with a timeline, root cause analysis using 5 Whys, at least three remediation items with owners, and a stakeholder communication plan.
steps: Gather metrics, logs, and traces to build a precise timeline
Apply the 5 Whys to identify the root cause
List contributing factors and prioritize remediation by risk and effort
Assign owners and deadlines to each action item
Write a stakeholder summary in plain language
data.expectedOutcome: You should produce a complete postmortem that a manager, an engineer, and a stakeholder can all read and act on.

data.title: Summary
points: RCA focuses on systems, not individuals
5 Whys reveal systemic causes when applied rigorously
Every remediation item needs an owner and a deadline
Publish postmortems quickly while evidence is fresh
Communicate proactively with stakeholders throughout the incident
data.takeaway: A senior engineer treats every incident as a gift: a chance to make the system stronger. The quality of your postmortem is measured not by how well you explain the failure, but by how many action items you actually complete.
